# pLxIS-containing domains are biochemically flexible regulators of interferons and metabolism

**Authors:** Lauren M. Landau; Neha Chaudhary; Yun Chen Tien; Magdalena Rogozinska; Shakchhi Joshi; Conghui Yao; Joseph Crowley; Karthik Hullahalli; Ian W. Campbell; Matthew K. Waldor; Marcia Haigis; Jonathan C. Kagan

**Affiliations:** 1Division of Gastroenterology, Boston Children’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School; Boston, MA, USA. | 2Cambridge Research Center, AbbVie, Inc.; Cambridge, MA, USA. | 3Department of Cell Biology, Blavatnik Institute, Harvard Medical School; Boston, MA, USA. | 4Division of Infectious Diseases, Brigham & Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School; Boston, MA, USA. | 5Lead contact

## Abstract

Signal transduction proteins containing a pLxIS motif induce interferon responses central to antiviral immunity. Apart from their established roles in activating the interferon regulator factor (IRF) transcription factors, the existence of additional pathways and functions associated with the pLxIS motif is unknown. Using a synthetic biology-based platform, we identified two orphan pLxIS-containing proteins that stimulate interferon responses independent of all known pattern recognition receptor pathways. We further uncovered a diversity of pLxIS signaling mechanisms, where the pLxIS motif represents one component of a multi-motif signaling entity which has variable functions in activating IRF3, the TRAF6 ubiquitin ligase, IκB kinases, mitogen-activated protein kinases, and metabolic activities. The most diverse pLxIS signaling mechanisms were associated with highest antiviral activities in human cells. The flexibility of domains that regulate interferon signaling may explain their prevalence in nature.

## Abstract

Landau et al. report two proteins, IRSp53 and GMIP, that contain pLxIS motifs that stimulate type I interferon activities. When comparing these proteins to the pLxIS containing factors STING, TRIF, MAVS and TASL, a diversity of protein-specific mechanisms of interferon activation was uncovered.

## Abstract

## INTRODUCTION

Innate immune signal transduction pathways represent modular information transfer networks. Infection-related inputs flow through multi-protein signaling pathways to downstream outputs that govern immunity. These pathways are controlled by common sets of protein-based signaling domains, including the Toll-IL-1 Receptor-Resistance protein (TIR) domain, Death Domain, Caspase-activation and recruitment domain (CARD), Death Effector Domain (DED), and Pyrin Domain1. Diverse innate immune pathways use proteins containing these domains as signaling hubs to link microbial detection to host defense2–5. The generalizability of this theme, however, has limited application to other immune signaling pathway activities—namely type I interferon (IFN) responses and changes in cellular metabolism6–9.

Three principal pathways are responsible for most examples of IFN expression. These pathways include those activated by the Toll-like receptors (TLRs), RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs), and the cytosolic DNA sensor cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)3,10. The key proteins that regulate IFN expression downstream of these receptors are TRIF (or TASL), MAVS, and STING, respectively11–15. Upon receptor activation, these proteins oligomerize to form large complexes known as supramolecular organizing centers (SMOCs), which represent the signaling organelles of the innate immune system16–19.

MAVS, STING, TRIF, and TASL share no homologous domains that would predict their common IFN activity during infection. However, recent work has highlighted a 5 amino acid motif essential for IFN expression20. This motif consists of the residues pLxIS, where p represents a hydrophilic residue and x represents any amino acid. Upon phosphorylation of the serine within this motif by IκB kinase (IKK) family members, such as TBK1, the pLxIS motif becomes a recruitment site for IFN-inducing transcription factors of the IRF family21–23. Within an unstructured region of the C-terminal tail (CTT) of STING, an additional PLPLR motif proximal to the pLxIS motif is responsible for binding and activating TBK124,25. While MAVS and TRIF contain analogous motifs that mediate TBK1 activation, it is unclear whether TASL or other orphan pLxIS-containing proteins operate by similar mechanisms. Moreover, beyond the ability to activate IRF transcription factors, no other function for the pLxIS motif has been defined.

In this study, we explored the diversity of pLxIS functions using a synthetic biology-based system to isolate and study pLxIS motif activities. We expanded the spectrum of known IFN-inducing pLxIS containing proteins, and additionally identified an unexpected diversity of pLxIS-based signaling mechanisms. Beyond IRF transcription factor activation, pLxIS motifs present in distinct proteins activated the ubiquitin ligase TRAF6, IKKs, mitogen activated protein kinases (MAPKs), aerobic glycolysis, and other metabolic activities. The most complex signaling entities represented the most robust mediators of antiviral immunity. These findings establish pLxIS-containing domains as commonly used and biochemically flexible regulators of IFNs and metabolism.

## RESULTS

### A synthetic biology-based approach to define signaling domain activities

Due to the diversity of biological variables associated with cross-pathway comparisons, it can be challenging to compare the activities of common signaling domains present in distinct proteins. To resolve this issue in the context of pLxIS domain biology, we employed a reductionist synthetic system that appends putative domains onto a chemically-oligomerizable protein-based scaffold 26. This approach was taken previously to study STING signaling, when we appended multiple copies of the STING CTT onto an FKBP scaffold that can be dimerized by the small molecule B/B26. To determine if a single CTT was sufficient to signal, the 39-amino acid CTT of STING was fused to a scaffold consisting of four copies of FKBP (Figure 1A and Table S1). Addition of B/B to immortalized bone marrow-derived macrophages (iBMDMs) expressing the FKBP-STING construct, hereafter referred to as a nanomachine, resulted in protein oligomerization. Oligomerization was evident as laddered multimers by native-PAGE or multiple specks within cells by fluorescence microscopy (Figures S1A and S1B). B/B-induced oligomerization of the STING nanomachine promoted the time-dependent induction of IFN responses, with expression of ifnb transcripts and phosphorylation of STAT1 observed within 2 hours. At later times, expression of IFN stimulated genes (ISGs) encoding the protein viperin (Rsad2) and the chemokine IP-10 (Cxcl10) were observed, as was IP-10 secretion (Figures S1C and S1D). Within minutes of B/B treatment, the STING CTT stimulated the activation of the kinase TBK1 (Figure 1B). The amounts of IP-10, IFN-β, and IFN-α secreted upon STING nanomachine activation were higher than those produced upon stimulation with the cGAS agonist poly(dA:dT) (Figure 1C). Engineering a nanomachine to contain the full-length STING protein (excluding the transmembrane domains) did not increase IP-10, viperin, or STAT1 levels beyond what was observed with the 39 amino acid CTT (Figures S1E-F). Titrating B/B to lower doses only decreased the full-length STING signaling capacity relative to the CTT (Figure S1E). These findings suggest that the STING CTT represents the entire IFN-inducing entity.

To determine if the pLxIS-containing domains from MAVS and TRIF could be similarly studied, we designed analogous FKBP-based nanomachines (Figure 1A and Table S1). B/B treatment of iBMDMs expressing the TRIF and MAVS nanomachines promoted IP-10 release, viperin production, STAT1 phosphorylation, and STAT1 production (Figure 1D). We performed RNA-sequencing of iBMDMs expressing the STING, TRIF, and MAVS nanomachines after B/B treatment. Analysis of the enriched gene ontology (GO) terms associated with genes induced by the STING CTT revealed upregulation of transcriptional programs such as cytokine production, PRR signaling, inflammatory response, and response to biotic stimulus (Figure S2A). Comparison of the STING nanomachine activities to iBMDMs treated with the STING agonist DMXAA demonstrated that the CTT was sufficient to recapitulate the transcriptome of its endogenous signaling pathway, only with faster kinetics (Figure S2B). Similarly, the MAVS and TRIF pLxIS-containing nanomachines induced comparable transcriptional programs to treatment with LPS and 3p-hpRNA, respectively (Figure S2C).

To identify features of each domain necessary to mediate IFN responses, mutational analysis was performed. Truncating the 183 N-terminal amino acids of the TRIF domain, while leaving the pLxIS motif intact, diminished B/B-induced IFN responses (Figures 1A, 1E, and S1F). Similarly, truncating the 10 C-terminal amino acids of the MAVS domain abolished IFN responses (Figures 1A, 1E, and S1F). To further define regions of the TRIF N-terminus required for signaling, we performed a series of smaller truncations. Truncated mutants of up to the first 143 amino acids of TRIF retained IFN signaling capacity, while those lacking residues 1–163 had diminished IFN signaling (Figures 1F and S1G). Thus, the globular N-terminal 143-amino acid domain of TRIF is not required for IFN signaling.

The transcription factor IRF3 also contains a pLxIS motif20. Given that IRF3 is not considered a signaling entity and cannot recruit TBK1, we would expect that oligomerization would be insufficient for IFN activation. Indeed, we found that iBMDMs expressing nanomachines appended with IRF3 were able to oligomerize but unable to undergo B/B-induced IFN induction (Figure S1H).

To further explore this concept, we generated nanomachines composed of the pLxIS-containing region, the C-terminal half, or the full-length version of TASL. None of these constructs generated IFN responses in iBMDMs upon B/B treatment (Figures 1G-H). As TASL has only been studied genetically in human cells, this finding prompted us to examine endogenous TASL signaling in the TLR pathway of iBMDMs. We generated TASL-deficient iBMDMs and, consistent with work in human cells13, observed a significant diminishment in IP-10 secretion in response to R848 and CpG DNA treatment (Figure 1J). This defect in IP-10 secretion in TASL-deficient cells was rescued by expression of a TASL transgene (Figures 1J and S1I).

A distinction between endogenous TASL signaling and nanomachine signaling is that the former occurs in concert with TLR-MyD88-mediated IKK family activation13. It was therefore possible that the TASL nanomachine failed to induce IFNs because TASL lacks a kinase activation motif needed to induce pLxIS signaling. To test this idea, we appended the PLPLR motif of STING to the C-terminal pLxIS-containing region of TASL within the nanomachine. Interestingly, this TASL-PLPLR fusion nanomachine induced IFN signaling upon B/B stimulation (Figures 1G-H). As expected from the PLPLR functions within STING25, the TASL-PLPLR nanomachine activated TBK1 but not IKKα/β phosphorylation (Figure 1I). These data suggest that, in contrast to the other IFN-inducing pLxIS proteins, TASL does not contain a kinase activation motif needed for signaling.

Based on this finding, we examined TASL-PLPLR activities in the context of endogenous TASL signaling, and determined if MyD88 served additional roles beyond providing kinase activation. We reconstituted MyD88-deficient cells with wild-type TASL, a TASL-PLPLR fusion, or a fusion of TASL with the IKK-binding site of NEMO. We found that wild-type TASL was unable to signal in response to R848 or CpG DNA in MyD88-deficient cells (Figure 1K). Notably, both TASL fusion proteins containing kinase activation motifs induced viperin production and STAT1 phosphorylation in MyD88-deficient cells upon R848 or CpG DNA stimulation (Figure 1K). These data suggest that TLR7–9, independent of MyD88, can engage TASL, but that the IKK activity stimulated by MyD88 is needed for the pLxIS within TASL to signal. This latter activity can be bypassed by engineering TASL to contain its own kinase activation motif (Figure 1K).

### A genetic screen expands the IFN-inducing pLxIS-containing domain family

Within the human and mouse genomes, 15 proteins contain uncharacterized pLxIS motifs that are conserved across diverse mammalian species20. Based on the insufficiency of the pLxIS motifs within MAVS, STING, TRIF, and TASL to induce IFN activities, it is challenging to predict the signaling potential of these proteins bioinformatically. To determine if these orphan pLxIS motif-containing proteins regulate IFN activities, we reasoned that oligomerization would reveal their signaling capacity. We engineered FKBP-based nanomachines appended with putative pLxIS-containing domains from each of these proteins (Table S1). Thirteen of the proteins we screened displayed no evidence of B/B-induced IFN activities in iBMDMs, whereas two nanomachines induced IP-10 release, viperin production, and STAT1 phosphorylation (Figures 2A and S1J). These two nanomachines were comprised of the pLxIS-containing domains from the proteins IRSp53 and GMIP. Both proteins are members of the BAR domain family, which regulates membrane curvature and cytoskeleton remodeling27–29. We screened an additional 12 proteins in the BAR domain family that contain pLxIS motifs conserved among mice and humans, yet none promoted B/B-induced IFN responses (Figure S3A). To further demonstrate the signaling capacity of the pLxIS-containing domains from IRSp53 and GMIP, we measured the upregulation of Ifnb, Rsad2, and Cxcl10 expression, and the secretion of IFN-β and IFN-α (Figures 2B-C). Both nanomachines induced all examined IFN outputs, with IRSp53 exhibiting greater magnitudes and faster kinetics than GMIP (Figures 2B-C).

RNA-sequencing of iBMDMs expressing the GMIP, IRSp53, MAVS, STING, and TRIF nanomachines revealed a consensus among the top differentially expressed genes (Figure 2D). All five pLxIS-containing domains upregulated a common set of genes associated with GO terms involved in the cellular response to virus, regulation of cytokine production, and response to IFN-β (Figure 2E). Representative transcripts were validated by RT-qPCR, illustrating the ability of all five domains to induce Ccl5 and Isg15 expression (Figure 2F). Thus, the pLxIS-containing domains of IRSp53 and GMIP induce similar IFN responses upon synthetic oligomerization as the known IFN stimulatory domains.

### The pLxIS motif can mediate kinase activation and transcription factor recruitment

Within MAVS, STING, and TRIF, the pLxIS motif is phosphorylated by TBK120,25. To probe pLxIS phosphorylation in a cell-free system, we generated recombinant nanomachines purified from E. coli and recombinant GST-tagged TBK1 purified from Sf9 cells (Figure S3B). We observed phosphorylation of the STING nanomachine on S365 by TBK1 (Figure S3C). This phosphorylation corresponded to an upward mobility shift in the total FKBP band by western blot (Figure S3C). We observed a similar upward shift in FKBP upon addition of TBK1 to the GMIP, IRSp53, MAVS, and TRIF nanomachines, but not to empty FKBP scaffolds (Figures 3A-B). This shift was reversed by the addition of λ-phosphatase (Figure 3A). Recombinant full-length GMIP and IRSp53 also underwent an upward shift in mobility upon TBK1 addition (Figure S3D). The GMIP, IRSp53, and STING nanomachines were analyzed by LC-MS/MS for peptide modifications. Analysis of the modified peptides revealed that the pLxIS serine of all three proteins was phosphorylated upon TBK1 addition (Figure 3C and Table S2). Several other serines and threonines were phosphorylated within the larger domain, including a serine cluster several residues upstream of the pLxIS (S354/S357) that plays a role in STING signaling30 (Figure 3C). However, several proximal serines remained unmodified, such as S348 in STING, S262 in IRSp53, or S19 in GMIP (Figure 3C). Mutation of the pLxIS serine to alanine in the IRSp53 (S269A) and GMIP (S31A) nanomachines partially or fully inhibited the upward shift associated with TBK1 addition (Figure 3B).

The phosphorylated serine within the pLxIS motifs of MAVS, STING, and TRIF is necessary for IFN induction20,24. The signaling domains acted accordingly within nanomachines, where pLxIS to pLxIA mutations diminished IP-10 release, viperin production, and STAT1 phosphorylation (Figures S3E-F). Similarly, mutation of the N, L, I, and S residues within the pLxIS motifs of IRSp53 and GMIP abolished IFN responses (Figures 3D and S3G). RNA-seq analysis revealed a set of pLxIS-dependent genes that represent GO pathways including innate immune response, regulation of cytokine production, response to virus, and response to IFN-β (Figures S4A and S4B). A subset of genes were induced by the pLxIA mutants of IRSp53 and GMIP, uncovering pLxIS-independent pathways involved in the regulation of chemotaxis and vasculature (Figures S4A and S4B). For example, the expression of the chemokine receptor Cxcr4 and the vasculogenesis regulator Egfl7 were induced by the wild-type and mutant domains, but not an empty FKBP scaffold (Figure S4C).

Consistent with the idea that the pLxIS motif acts in tandem with other adjacent motifs24,25, mutation of the second leucine within the TBK1 binding motif of STING, PLPLR, diminished IFN responses (Figures S3E-F). Similarly, mutation of residue L193 in TRIF31, or the second glutamic acid (E433) within the TRAF6-binding motif, PEENEY, in MAVS32,33 phenocopied pLxIS mutations (Figures S3E-F). The pLxIS motifs of IRSp53 and GMIP were also insufficient to drive IFN expression, as either N-terminal or C-terminal truncations of the domains used in the nanomachines eliminated B/B-induced IFN responses (Figures 3E and S3H).

The pLxIS motif has been exclusively described as a mediator of transcription factor recruitment, as opposed to kinase activation25,33–35. Consistent with this model, pLxIS mutations in STING (S365A) or MAVS (S418A) did not impact TBK1 phosphorylation (Figure 3F). In contrast, L373A mutation in the PLPLR motif in STING and the E433A mutation in the PEENEY motif in MAVS abolished TBK1 phosphorylation (Figure 3F). This observation effectively subdivides the activities of these domains between TBK1 activation and IRF3 activation. Interestingly, mutation of the pLxIS motifs within IRSp53 (S269A) or GMIP (S31A) prevented TBK1 phosphorylation, suggesting a contribution of the pLxIS motif to kinase activation (Figure 3G). Immunoprecipitations of the nanomachines supported this model, as we detected a complex between endogenous TBK1 and all 5 domains (Figure 3H). The interaction between TBK1 and the IRSp53 and GMIP domains was abolished upon pLxIA mutation, while this interaction was unaffected by pLxIA mutations in MAVS, STING, and TRIF (Figure 3H). The pLxIS motifs in IRSp53 and GMIP therefore mediate TBK1 activation. Accordingly, if the pLxIS motif in IRSp53 (which activates TBK1) was replaced by the pLxIS motif in STING (which cannot activate TBK1), the resulting IRSp53 nanomachine could not induce IFN responses or activate TBK1 (Figures 3J and S5A). Conversely, replacement of the STING nanomachine pLxIS motif with the IRSp53 pLxIS motif maintained IFN signaling and TBK1 phosphorylation (Figures 3J and S5A). Yet, the IRSp53 pLxIS motif is unable to rescue signaling in the STING L373A mutant, suggesting it is necessary but not sufficient for IFN induction (Figures 3J and S5A). Within macrophages, MAVS, STING, and TRIF signal through IRF3 to mediate IFN expression20,22. The IRSp53 nanomachine also induced IRF3 phosphorylation, akin to the MAVS and STING nanomachines, after 30 minutes of B/B treatment (Figure 3I).

Engagement of TBK1 by STING is facilitated by the flexible nature of the CTT, which inserts between two TBK1 subunits19,25. A disorder analysis on the 40 amino acids surrounding the pLxIS motif using the IUPred3 and Anchor algorithms revealed that all proteins with demonstrated IFN activity (except TASL) contained disordered pLxIS-containing regions (Figure S5B). This disorder is further demonstrated by the predicted AlphaFold structures of each protein, where the signaling domains are illustrated as predominantly unstructured regions (Figure S5B). Thus, IRSp53 and GMIP exhibit similar features of IFN induction within the nanomachine system including: 1) protein oligomerization, 2) a requirement for a pLxIS motif plus adjacent residues, and 3) a disordered region of the protein (Figure S5D). However, it is insufficient to simply combine a pLxIS motif and a TBK1-binding motif within a disordered region, because fully synthetic nanomachines composed of these building blocks were unable to signal. For example, inserting the IRSp53 pLxIS motif and the STING PLPLR motif into the backbone of either the globular proteins RFP or Myoglobin, or the disordered regions of p27 or H3, did not generate detectable IFN responses (Figure S5E).

### pLxIS-containing domains use TBK1 to induce IFN and metabolic activities

Despite their common ability to activate TBK1, expression of the IRSp53 or GMIP nanomachines in TBK1- or IRF3-deficient iBMDMs revealed differences in their requirement for IFN expression. We found that TBK1 and IRF3 were required for IFN activities induced by the GMIP domain (Figures 4A and S5F). In contrast, signaling by the IRSp53 domain was intact in TBK1-deficient cells, even at lower doses of B/B (Figures 4A and S5F). Dependence of the IRSp53 domain on IRF3 was only observed at lower concentrations of B/B (Figure S6A). Similarly, pretreatment of cells with the TBK1/IKKε inhibitor MRT67307 abolished IP-10 release by the GMIP domain but not the IRSp53 domain (Figure 4B).

To determine the role of TBK1 in IRSp53-mediated signaling, we considered the activities of this kinase beyond IFN expression. In addition to mediating transcriptional programs, TBK1 promotes the induction of TLR-dependent glycolysis via the kinase AKT18,26,36,37. To assess glycolysis, we monitored the extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) resulting from the release of lactate (an end product of glycolysis). The IRSp53, MAVS, and STING signaling domains promoted glycolysis to an extent comparable to LPS treatment (Figure 4C). This glycolytic flux was prevented by the TBK1/IKKε inhibitor MRT67307, the AKT1 inhibitor GSK690693, or the hexokinase inhibitor 2-DG (Figure S6B). Similarly, ECAR was diminished in TBK1-deficient cells (Figure 4D). Thus, while TBK1 is variably required for pLxIS-induced IFN activities, this kinase is commonly required for glycolysis. However, TBK1 activation is not sufficient to stimulate glycolysis, as the TRIF and GMIP nanomachines did not induce this metabolic response upon B/B treatment (Figure 4C).

To explore other impacts on metabolism, we performed metabolite profiling on the intracellular contents of nanomachine-expressing iBMDMs stimulated with B/B for 1 or 24 hours. This analysis revealed classes of metabolites induced by all or subsets of the nanomachines (Figures S6C, S6E, and Table S3). For example, all five nanomachines promoted increased levels of succinate (Figure 4E), which can serve as an immunoregulatory signal38. Conversely, some metabolites were regulated by a single nanomachine, such as IRSp53-directed increase in the abundance of the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine39 (Figure 4E).

These findings raised the question of which metabolic pathways may contribute to IFN production. The IRSp53, MAVS, STING, and TRIF nanomachines all increased levels of D-glucose within cells, and inhibition with the glucose antagonist 2-DG diminished IP-10 production by each of these nanomachines (Figures 4F-G). All five nanomachines also caused a decrease in the intracellular ATP/ADP ratio, representing high demand for ATP and a loss in the energetic charge of the cell, favoring enhanced glycolysis40–42 (Figure 4G). Inhibition of ATP synthase by oligomycin inhibited IP-10 release, although to a lesser extent than 2-DG, suggesting a role for oxidative phosphorylation (Figure 4F). Similarly, α-ketoglutarate was increased by the GMIP, IRSp53, MAVS, and STING nanomachines, and inhibition with an antagonist of its upstream precursor glutamine43, 6-diazo-5-oxo-norleucine (DON), diminished IP-10 production (Figures 4F-G). Pyruvate metabolism, in contrast, was unaffected by any nanomachine activities, as we observed no changes in acetyl-CoA levels, and treatment with the mitochondrial pyruvate inhibitor UK5099 had no negative impact on IP-10 production (Figures 4G and S6D). Finally, in contrast to observations made in dendritic cells8, fatty acid metabolism did not appear to play a role in pLxIS signaling activities, as inhibition of either fatty acid synthesis by C75 or fatty acid oxidation by etomoxir did not impact IP-10 release by the nanomachines (Figure S6D). These data suggest that signaling by the five pLxIS-containing domains caused broad changes in metabolism, with the induction of glycolysis, ATP synthesis, and glutaminolysis revealed as important in mediating the bioenergetic demands of macrophages to induce IFN responses via pLxIS-containing domains.

### TRAF6 engagement by select pLxIS-containing domains diversifies downstream signaling pathways

TBK1 recruitment mechanisms vary among IFN adaptors; STING binds TBK1 directly while MAVS recruits TBK1 indirectly through members of the TRAF family of E3 ubiquitin ligases25,33,34,44. Expression of nanomachines in TRAF6-deficient immortalized fetal liver-derived macrophages (iFLDMs) revealed that the IRSp53 and MAVS domains required TRAF6 for IFN responses (Figures 5A, 5C, and S6F). In contrast, GMIP, STING and TRIF did not require TRAF6 for IFN induction (Figures 5A and 5C). Immunoprecipitations revealed interactions between TRAF6 and the domains of IRSp53 and MAVS, but not GMIP, STING or TRIF (Figure 5B). TRAF6 interacted with the MAVS and IRSp53 nanomachines before and after B/B treatment, indicating the formation of a pre-signaling complex (Figure 5B). We noted B/B-induced depletion of the TRAF6 bands in the input fractions, and hypothesized this resulted from poly-ubiquitination-induced upward smearing on the gel. Indeed, immunoprecipitations of the IRSp53 and MAVS nanomachines revealed a B/B-induced poly-ubiquitination of the complex, which was dependent on the presence of TRAF6 (Figure 5D).

We explored the possibility that TRAF6 recruitment diversifies the spectrum of innate immune pathways activated by subsets of pLxIS-containing domains45–47. While the GMIP and TRIF domains only activated TBK1, the STING domain activated TBK1 and induced phosphorylation of IKKα/β and the NF-κB p65 subunit. IRSp53 and MAVS, which both bind TRAF6, activated the widest spectrum of immune pathways, including TBK1, IKKα/β, NF-κB p65, and the p38 and JNK1 MAPKs (Figure 5E). We found that all pathways activated by the IRSp53 and MAVS nanomachines depended on TRAF6 (Figure 5F). Immunoprecipitations revealed that TRAF6 was required for TBK1 interactions with the IRSp53 and MAVS domains (Figure 5G). In contrast, the interactions between TBK1 and the GMIP, STING, and TRIF domains were not TRAF6-dependent (Figure 5G). As with TBK1 activation, the activation of NF-κB p65, p38, and JNK1 was abolished by the S269A mutation in IRSp53 (Figure 5H). Ingenuity pathway analysis (IPA) of the RNA-sequencing data indicated that, relative to GMIP and TRIF, the IRSp53, MAVS and STING nanomachines promote higher NF-κB and AP-1-regulated gene expression (Figure 5I). These data implicate TRAF6 as a master regulator of pLxIS signaling diversification.

### The IRSp53 and GMIP domains signal independently of known IFN pathways

Having explored the downstream signaling diversity of the IRSp53 and GMIP pLxIS domains, we determined if they played a role in the known IFN pathways. We found that endogenous IRSp53 and GMIP proteins were produced by iBMDMs but not upregulated by LPS treatment (Figure 6A). To determine if IRSp53 and GMIP were required for the ability of known innate immune pathways to induce IFNs, we generated cells deficient in IRSp53 or GMIP and stimulated with agonists of TLR4 (LPS), TLR9 (CpG DNA), cGAS (electroporated poly(dA:dT)), or RIG-I (electroporated 3p-hpRNA) (Figures 6B-D). Although IP-10 induction was slightly diminished in IRSp53- or GMIP-deficient cells electroporated with 3p-hpRNA, we observed no differences in viperin, phospho-STAT1, and total STAT1 abundance, and no PAMP-induced responses absolutely required these genes (Figures 6C-D). There were also no significant differences in IP-10 release at lower concentrations of LPS or CpG DNA (Figure S7A). Furthermore, doxycycline-induced overexpression of IRSp53 or GMIP did not affect LPS-induced IP-10 production (Figure 6E).

Having eliminated the requirement of IRSp53 and GMIP for multiple known innate immune pathways, we determined if known IFN-inducing adaptor proteins are required for IRSp53 or GMIP activities. We generated iBMDMs combinatorically deficient in MyD88 (to abolish TASL signaling), TRIF, STING, and MAVS; these cells are referred to as MTSM knockout (KO) cells. MTSM KO cells were unable to secrete IP-10 in response to CpG DNA, LPS, DMXAA, or the RLR-MAVS agonist Sendai virus; however, these cells responded normally to recombinant IFN-β (Figure 6F). The IRSp53 domain displayed no defects in STAT1 phosphorylation or viperin production in MTSM KO cells (Figure 6G). GMIP-induced responses were also intact in MTSM KO cells, although minor defects in STAT1 phosphorylation and viperin production were observed (Figure 6G). These observations remained consistent at lower doses of B/B (Figure S7B). These data suggest that IRSp53 and GMIP pLxIS-containing domains operate independently of known IFN-inducing pathways in macrophages.

Because BAR domain proteins are regulated by the actin cytoskeleton, membrane curvature, and GTPase activation, we tested the requirement of IRSp53 and GMIP in signaling downstream of pathogens and effectors that manipulate these processes. For example, enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) injects the intimin receptor Tir into host cells, which interacts with IRSp53 to mediate actin pedestal generation48. However, infection of IRSp53 or GMIP KO cells with Citrobacter rodentium, a murine model of EHEC49, did not impact IP-10 secretion, or result in IP-10 secretion independent of MAVS, MyD88, STING and TRIF (Figure S7C). Additionally, IRSp53 is involved in HIV particle assembly at the plasma membrane using the viral protein Gag50,51. Pseudotransduction of a virus-like particle (VLP) composed of Gag and VSV-G52 induced IP-10 secretion, but this process was unaltered in IRSp53- or GMIP-deficient cells (Figure S7C). To mitigate triggering known IFN pathways with infection systems, we tested for IFN induction by the overexpression of individual microbial effectors. No IP-10 secretion was observed upon doxycycline-induced expression of Gag, Tir, the S. Typhimurium protein SopE that activates Rho GTPases53,54, nor the Y. enterocolitica protein YopE that inhibits Rho GTPases55 (Figure S7D). Thus, IRSp53 and GMIP do not regulate IFN responses downstream of these tested pathogens or molecules.

Doxycycline-induced expression of wild-type IRSp53 or GMIP, phosphomimetic mutants of the pLxIS serine, mutations in the autoinhibitory domain, or co-expression with autoactivated forms of the Rho GTPases Cdc42 or Rac1 did not produce any detectable IFN responses (Figures S7E-F). To determine if the IRSp53 and GMIP pLxIS-containing domains were functional in the context of natural PAMP-induced oligomerization, we replaced the MAVS pLxIS-containing domain with the pLxIS-containing domain of IRSp53 or GMIP. MTSM KO cells reconstituted with wild-type MAVS, MAVSIRSp53 pLxIS chimeras, or MAVSGMIP pLxIS chimeras, but not MAVSΔpLxIS deletion mutants were able to induce IP-10 release, viperin production, and STAT1 phosphorylation upon 3p-hpRNA transfection (Figures 6H-I). Thus, the IFN activities of the IRSp53 and GMIP pLxIS-containing domains are functional in the context of natural MAVS CARD-mediated oligomerization.

### MAVS and IRSp53 signaling domains are the most potent agents of antiviral immunity

The diversity of pLxIS signaling mechanisms we uncovered raised the question of which activities are most beneficial for host defense. To address this, we studied antiviral immune responses in human lung A549 epithelial cells expressing each nanomachine. Akin to our observations in iBMDMs, IRSp53, MAVS, STING, and TRIF induced a variety of IFN-associated factors, including the expression of IFNB1 and ISG15, secretion of IP-10, production of viperin, and phosphorylation of STAT1 (Figures 7A and 7B). In contrast, the GMIP domain was unable to induce IFN responses in these cells (Figures 7A and 7B). To assess host defense, cells were pretreated for 2 hours with B/B and then infected with vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) or influenza A virus (IAV) PR8 H1N1. The STING and TRIF domains restricted VSV and IAV replication to a modest extent, as assessed by intracellular levels of VSV L transcripts or PR8 NA transcripts, and extracellular plaque forming units (pfu) (Figures 7C and 7D). In contrast, the IRSp53 and MAVS domains were highly protective, resulting in log-based decreases in replication of both viruses (Figures 7C and 7D).

To determine the role of TBK1, cells were pretreated with the TBK1/IKKε inhibitor MRT67307 prior to B/B induction. Pretreatment with MRT67307 attenuated the antiviral activities of the IRSp53 and MAVS domains (Figure 7E). Since we found TBK1 to contribute to IFN activities and glycolysis, we determined the relative role of these processes. While IRSp53-mediated IFN activity was independent of TBK1 in iBMDMs, IP-10 secretion induced by the MAVS and IRSp53 domains in A549 cells was abolished by MRT67307 pretreatment, suggesting a cell type-specific requirement for TBK1/IKKε in IFN induction56 (Figure 7F). Pretreatment with 2-DG also prevented maximal antiviral activities of the IRSp53 and MAVS domains (Figure 7G), suggesting that the defensive activities of these domains are mediated, in part, by their glycolytic functions. In the absence of B/B treatment, neither 2-DG nor MRT67307 impacted the replicative abilities of VSV or IAV, consistent with the abilities of these viruses to prevent innate immune responses during infection57,58.

VSV and IAV prevent IFN responses via distinct mechanisms. While the M protein of VSV generally inhibits host transcription and translation, the NS1 protein of IAV can inhibit the viral RNA receptor RIG-I57,58. Because our nanomachines bypass receptor activation, we asked whether B/B treatment differentially affects VSV versus IAV IFN inhibition. Indeed, VSV infection prevented substantial secretion of IP-10 and expression of ISG15 induced by the IRSp53 and MAVS nanomachines, but IAV infection did not affect these IFN-associated activities (Figure 7H). Accordingly, nanomachine-mediated restriction of VSV replication was only evident with B/B administration prior to infection, whereas IAV replication was prevented by the IRSp53 and MAVS nanomachines even if B/B was administered 2 hours post-infection (Figure 7I). These data establish the functional significance of signaling diversification by pLxIS-containing domains in the context of host defense.

## DISCUSSION

Bioinformatic approaches are increasingly utilized to identify proteins with biochemical properties of interest. However, understanding the function of orphan proteins is hindered by a lack of experimental systems to stimulate putative activities. By taking advantage of oligomer-directed signaling pathway activation, our synthetic biology-based approach addressed this problem. This approach enabled not only the definition of common and distinct activities of MAVS, STING and TRIF, but allowed elucidation of the split domain mechanism of TASL and identification of IFN regulatory domains within IRSp53 and GMIP. However, the negative results of the nanomachine screens are not necessarily conclusive, as proteins with natural IFN signaling capacity may utilize a split domain mechanism akin to TASL or may be non-functional in our synthetic system for technical reasons.

The diversification of individual domains was showcased by differential abilities to induce glycolysis and engage TRAF6, with consequential effects on downstream pathway activation and antiviral activities. Additionally, TASL is unique in its mechanism of physically separating two coordinated motifs between proteins, a mechanism utilized by other proteins such as the split pleckstrin homology (PH) domain of phospholipase C-δ159. Unexpectedly, TASL did not require MyD88 to signal if another source of kinase activation was provided. How TASL is engaged by TLRs in a MyD88-independent manner has yet to be explored, but it could interact with TLRs or TIRAP60. Indeed, evidence suggests TLR9-dependent, MyD88-independent pathways regulate signaling in systemic lupus erythematosus61, a disease TASL is genetically associated with13. Further diversity was observed in the use of the pLxIS motif as a transcription factor recruitment site20 or as an enzyme recruitment site. The additional TBK1 phosphorylation sites on IRSp53 and GMIP may play a role in this mechanism, and help explain why truncations distal from the pLxIS motif abolish IFN signaling capacity. We speculate that the disordered nature of these domains is a mechanism that facilitates evolvability, leading to the diversity of signaling activities we have described.

Our identification of the pLxIS-containing domains of IRSp53 and GMIP is notable because these proteins have only been studied in the context of their membrane curvature and actin cytoskeletal functions as BAR domain proteins27,62–64. One noteworthy feature of BAR domains is their ability to undergo antiparallel dimerization and form higher order oligomers65,66. Thus, these proteins resemble characteristic innate immune signaling proteins in their composition of an oligomerization domain and a regulatory domain. An intriguing question is that of the potential function of IRSp53- or GMIP-mediated IFN regulation. As IRSp53 and GMIP are not required for IFN responses downstream of TLRs, cGAS, or RLRs, we speculate a number of possibilities. These proteins: 1) could be involved in tonic IFN signaling in specific organs, 2) could regulate IFN expression in a cell type other than macrophages, 3) could function as negative regulatory decoys, or 4) could only induce IFN responses in the context of MAVS- or nanomachine-mediated oligomerization. It is our opinion that the latter possibility is unlikely due to the capacity of the nanomachines to recapitulate the signaling functions of MAVS, STING, and TRIF, as well as the fact that IRSp53 and GMIP derive from the same family of oligomerizing proteins. Also noteworthy is that, similar to MAVS, STING, and TRIF, the evolutionary conservation of the pLxIS motifs in IRSp53 and GMIP tracks among animal species that contain IFN genes (Table S4). Organisms such as the Swiftwater hydra Hydra vulgaris, which do not encode IFN genes, contain IRSp53 homologues that do not contain a pLxIS motif (Table S4).

In summary, this study revealed unexpected diversity in the operation of a commonly used innate immune signaling domain. This finding provides a mandate to carefully explore the homology of other commonly used innate immune signaling domains in nature, which may prove more diverse than we think.

### LIMITATIONS OF THE STUDY

While this study identified an unexpected diversity of pLxIS signaling mechanisms, a central limitation related to the natural function of IRSp53 and GMIP. These proteins were not previously known to regulate IFN signaling, yet their pLxIS motifs are able to induce IFN and ISG expression. Our analysis of cells deficient in IRSp53 or GMIP did not reveal a requirement for either protein for the innate immune responses tested. It is possible that an agonist (yet to be discovered) mediates IRSp53- or GMIP-induced IFN activities. Alternatively, these proteins may regulate IFN responses in cell types we have yet to explore. Future work in animal models lacking these factors may provide insight into the endogenous innate immune functions of these proteins.

### EXPERIMENTAL MODEL AND STUDY PARTICIPANT DETAILS

#### Cell culture

Immortalized bone marrow derived macrophages (iBMDMs) or immortalized fetal liver derived macrophages (iFLDMs) were cultured in DMEM containing 10% FBS, Penicillin and Streptomycin (Pen+Strep), and supplements of L-glutamine (2 mM) and sodium pyruvate (1 mM). These cells were washed in PBS and then detached in culture flasks with 0.25% Trypsin. All cells were passaged 1:10 every 2–3 days to prevent overcrowding and media acidification.

### METHOD DETAILS

#### Construct Preparation

All FKBP-pLxIS constructs were designed with an N-terminal 3xFLAG-tag and a GAGAGA linker sequence between the 4xFKBP and the pLxIS-containing domain. The fusion cDNAs were synthesized as gBLOCKs via IDT. All synthetic DNA sequences were optimized to avoid internal repeats and for optimal expression in murine cells via the IDT online program. For expression in iBMDMs, FKBP-pLxIS constructs were restriction digested by BglII and NotI restriction nucleases and inserted into the pMSCV-IRES-GFP vector at BglII/NotI sites. The mutant and truncated alleles were generated using the Q5 site-directed mutagenesis kit.

For inducible expression upon retroviral transduction, all constructs were inserted into the pRETROX Tre3G plasmid (Clontech). All pathogen effector genes were synthesized as gBLOCKS via IDT. These were restriction digested by BamHI and EcoRI restriction nucleases and inserted into the pRETROX Tre3G vector at BamHI/EcoRI sites.

For recombinant protein expression, all constructs were restriction digested by BamHI and EcoRI restriction nucleases and inserted into the pET28a vector at BamHI/EcoRI sites. The exception was for expression of TBK1, the TBK1 sequence was designed with an N-terminal GST tag linked to the TBK1 sequence via a TEV cleavage site. This construct was digested by BamHI and XhoI restriction nucleases and inserted into the pFastBac vector at BamHI/XhoI sites.

#### Transfection and Retroviral Transduction

To generate cell lines stably expressing transgenes, retroviral particles were produced by transfecting 293T cells with the plasmids pCL-Eco, pCMV-VSV-G, and pMSCV-IRES-GFP containing the gene of interest. For lentiviral-mediated expression of pLenti-CRISPRv2 vectors, lentiviral particles were produced by transfecting 293T cells with plasmids psPAX2, pCMV-VSV-G, and pLenti-CRISPRv2 lentiviral vector containing the gRNA of interest. For lentiviral-mediated expression of Tet3G vectors, lentiviral particles were produced by transfecting 293T cells with plasmids psPAX2, pCMV-VSV-G, and pRETROX Tre3G lentiviral vector containing the gene of interest.

Plasmids were transfected into HEK293T cells in 10 cm dishes at a confluency of 70% with lipofectamine 2000 and media was changed 6 hr post transfection and viral supernatants were collected 24 hr post media change. Viral supernatants were spun at 400 x g to remove cellular debris, then passed through a 0.45 mm PVDF filter via syringe. Polybrene was added to the filtered supernatants (5 μg/ml), and the supernatants were then used to transduce iBMDMs via spin-fection at 1250 x g for 60 min at 30°C. The cell lines expressing pMSCV-IRES-GFP constructs were sorted based on GFP expression to ensure comparable levels of transgene expression. For gRNA-CRISPR expression, pLenti-CRISPRv2 plasmids were transduced into iBMDMs and consequent cell lines were selected by puromycin (10 μg/ml) 3 days after transduction. For TET3G mediated dox expression, pRETROX Tre3G plasmids were transduced into iBMDMs expressing the pRETROX Tet3G cassette (selected by 1.5 mg/mL G-418), and consequent cell lines stably expressing TRE3G constructs were selected by puromycin (10 μg/ml) 3 days after transduction.

#### Generation of KO iBMDMs

To generate iBMDMs deficient for TBK1, IRF3, or STING (in a pre-existing MyD88/TRIF-deficient background), gRNAs against the gene of interest were cloned into the pLentiCRISPRv2vector and transduced into iBMDMs as described above. These cells were selected with puromycin (10 μg/ml) 3 days after transduction and then were further single cell cloned by limiting serial dilution to yield clonal populations of homozygous knock-outs. The colonies were expanded and then validated for loss of protein expression by Western Blot analysis.

To generate iBMDMs deficient for IRSp53, GMIP, or TASL, sgRNAs against the gene were electroporated into cells expressing Cas9. sgRNAs were designed using IDT’s Cas9 guide RNA design tool. Electroporation was conducted using the Neon transfection machine, pipette, tips, and associated commercial buffers (ThermoFisher Scientific). 1.2E6 cells were suspended in 120 μL of R buffer from the Neon transfection kit. 2 μL of 100 μM sgRNA were added to the cell suspension prior to electroporation. Cells were drawn into the Neon transfection pipette and electroporated with the parameters of Voltage 1400, pulse width 10 ms, and pulse number 2. These cells were further single cell cloned by limiting serial dilution to yield clonal populations of homozygous knock-outs, which were validated by Western Blot analysis. To generate the MyD88/TRIF/STING/MAVS-deficient cells, sgRNAs against MAVS were electroporated into the pre-existing Cas9-expressing MyD88/TRIF/STING-deficient cells.

To validate TASL-deficient cells, genomic DNA was extracted from single cell clones using the Wizard Genomic DNA Purification Kit. PCR was performed on the extracted genomic DNA using oligos flanking the TASL gene site, and the PCR product was analyzed by Sanger sequencing and knock-out efficiency was evaluated using the Synthego Interference of CRISPR Edits (ICE) platform.

#### Stimulation with PAMPs and Small Molecules

The following ligands were added to the extracellular media: B/B (1 μM), LPS (1 μg/mL), DMXAA (10 μg/mL), R848 (10 μg/mL), CpG ODN 1826 (2 μM), CpG ODN 1585 (1 μM), IFN-β (100 ng/μL), doxycycline (2 μg/mL).

For transfection of CpG ODN 1585 (1 μM final) with DOTAP, 2 μL of 500 μM ODN 1585 was mixed with 20 μL of 1 μg/mL DOTAP in 78 μL opti-MEM for 15 minutes. The 100 μL mixture was then added to 900 μL of complete DMEM and added to cells.

For electroporation of 3p-hpRNA (1 μg/mL) or poly(dA:dT) (1 μg/mL), 1 μL of 1 mg/mL ligand was added to 100 μL cells in the R buffer. Cells were drawn into the Neon transfection pipette and electroporated with the parameters of Voltage 1400, pulse width 10 ms, and pulse number 2. Cells were then dispensed into 900 μL complete DMEM in a 12-well plate.

For pretreatment with metabolic inhibitors, cells were pretreated for 30 minutes with the following working concentrations: 25 mM 2-DG, 100 μM UK5099, 200 μM etomoxir, 10 μM DON, 1 μM oligomycin, 200 μM C75.

#### Gene Expression Analysis

RNA was isolated from cell cultures using the PureLink RNA Mini Kit (Invitrogen). Purified RNA was analyzed for gene expression on a CFX384 real time cycler (Bio-Rad) using TaqMan RNA-to-CT 1-Step Kit (Applied Biosystems) with probes specific for mouse Rsad2, Cxcl10, Ifnβ1, Ccl5, Isg15, Cxcr4, Egfl7, and Tbp. Because the TaqMan probes for Ifnβ1 and Isg15 do not span exon-exon boundaries, these samples were treated with the on-column PureLink DNase Kit during RNA isolation. Tbp was used as the reference gene.

To determine human and viral mRNA levels, RNA was isolated from cell lysates using the PureLink RNA Mini Kit. 2 ug of purified RNA was converted to cDNA using the High-capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (Applied Biosystems). The cDNA was analyzed for gene expression on a CFX384 real time cycler using the iTaq Universal SYBR Green Supermix (BioRad) with primers specific to human IFNβ1, ISG15, and GAPDH, and viral primers specific to VSV L and IAV PR8 NA.

#### ELISA

Cell culture supernatants were cleared of cell debris by spinning 96 well plates at 400 x g for 5 min, and the supernatants were transferred to new 96 well plates. Concentrations of mouse and human IP-10 were measured using the R&D DuoSet ELISA kits, mouse IFNβ was measured using the LumiKine Xpress mIFNβ 2.0 Kit, and mouse IFNα was measured using the VeriKine ELISA Kit.

#### Western Blotting and Immunoprecipitation

For western analysis, 0.5 × 106 iBMDMs were seeded in 12 well plates and stimulated with ligands for indicated periods, and subsequently lysed in 375 μL Laemmli buffer (12 mM TRIS pH 6.8, 5% glycerol, 1% SDS, 0.02% Bromophenol Blue, 1% β-mercaptoethanol). Lysates were incubated at 100°C for 5 min. Lysates were passed through a BD 1 mL sub-Q syringe attached to a 26G needle to reduce viscosity. 25 μL of individual samples were separated by SDS-PAGE followed by western analysis. All primary antibodies were diluted 1:1000 in Tris-buffered saline pH 7.6 with 0.1% Tween-20 (with the exception of pIRF3, which was diluted in phosphate-buffered saline with 0.1% Tween-20).

For nanomachine immunoprecipitation, 10 × 106 iBMDMs were stimulated with 1 μM B/B for indicated times, washed with PBS twice, and subsequently lysed in 1 mL of lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, 5% Glycerol, and 1% NP4078. The complete mini EDTA-free protease inhibitor and the phosphatase inhibitors β-glycerophosphate disodium salt hydrate (25 mM), sodium fluoride (10 mM), and sodium orthovanadate (1 mM) were added prior to cell lysis. Lysates were spun at top speed for 15 min at a table-top centrifuge at 4°C. The cleared supernatants were collected and 50 μL of the supernatants was saved as sample inputs. 40 μL of anti-FLAG M2 Affinity gel was added to the remaining supernatants, which were incubated overnight at 4°C on a nutator. The beads containing the protein complexes were then washed 3 times with 500 μL of lysis buffer, and 50 μL of 100 ng/μL 3x FLAG Peptide was added to elute the protein complexes. The beads were spun down and the supernatants were transferred to new tubes. Laemmli buffer was added, and the samples were separated by SDS-PAGE and analyzed by western blot.

#### Recombinant Protein Expression and Purification

FKBP-pLxIS, IRSp53, and GMIP constructs for in vitro phosphorylation assays were expressed in E. coli. Chemically competent Rosetta (DE3) pLysS cells were transformed with the pET28a plasmid encoding the protein of interest and plated on LB agar plates with kanamycin (25 μg/mL). Overnight precultures were inoculated with multiple colonies and grown at 30°C and 250 rpm in 2×YT medium containing kanamycin (25 μg/mL) and chloramphenicol (50 μg/ml). Large expression cultures of 50 to 500 mL were inoculated with overnight cultures at a ratio of 1:100 and incubated at 37°C and 250 rpm until the optical density at 600 nm (OD600) reached a value between 0.6 and 0.8. After cooling on ice for 15 minutes, protein expression was induced by adding isopropyl-β-D-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) to a final concentration of 0.25 mM, and expression was allowed to proceed overnight at 18 °C. Bacterial pellets were collected by centrifugation at 5,000 x g for 10 min at 4 °C.

For expression of GST-TBK1 in Sf9 insect cells, chemically competent DH10Bac cells were transformed with a pFastBac vector encoding the protein of interest and cells were plated on LB agar plates supplemented with 25 μg/mL kanamycin, 10 μg/mL tetracycline, 7 μg/mL gentamicin, 50 μg/mL X-Gal and 40 μg/mL IPTG and incubated for 48 h at 37 °C for blue/white screening. 20 mL of LB medium with 25 μg/mL kanamycin, 10 μg/mL tetracycline, 7 μg/mL gentamicin was inoculated with one positive (white) colony and incubated overnight at 37 °C and 250 rpm. Bacmid DNA was isolated using buffer components from the GeneJET Plasmid Miniprep kit and precipitated using isopropanol. The DNA pellet was washed once with 70% ethanol, air dried and resuspended in 40 μL of sterile, ultrapure water. 10 μL of resuspended bacmid DNA was diluted with 100 μL of Hyclone SFX insect cell medium. 10 μL of CellFectin II transfection reagent was mixed with 100 μL of medium and added to the DNA mixture. After incubating at room temperature for 30 min, 100 μL of the transfection mix was added dropwise to 0.8 × 106 Sf9 cells seeded in a six-well plate in 3 mL of medium. After 3–4 days of incubation at 28°C and 120 rpm, the baculovirus-containing supernatant was collected by centrifuging down the debris at 3500 x g, filtered using a 0.45 μm syringe filter and stored at 4 °C. To amplify the initial P1 virus, Sf9 cells were grown at a density of 1.0 × 106 cells per ml in a total volume of 25 mL, infected with 2 mL of the P1 virus and incubated at 28°C and 120 rpm. After 3 days, virus was collected by centrifuging the cells at 3500 x g for 5 min and taking off the baculovirus-containing supernatant, which was then passed through a 0.45 μm syringe filter and stored at 4 °C. For protein expression, 1 L of Sf9 cells were grown to a density of 1.5 × 106 cells per mL in a suspension culture, infected with 10 mL of the amplified virus and incubated at 28°C and 120 rpm. Once cells reached a size of >14 μm and underwent proliferation arrest (typically 48–72 hours), cells were collected by centrifugation at 1,000 x g for 15 min.

To purify recombinant proteins, bacterial or insect cell pellets were resuspended in resuspension buffer (25 mM HEPES-NaOH (pH 7.4), 500 mM NaCl and 10 mM imidazole) and lysed by ultrasonication. Cell lysates were clarified by centrifugation for 30–45 min at 20,000 x g at 4 °C and then added onto a gravity-flow column containing a bed of nickel–nitrilotriacetic acid (Ni-NTA) agarose beads. The beads were washed with at least 10 bed volumes of wash buffer (25 mM HEPES (pH 7.4), 500 mM NaCl and 25 mM imidazole) and the bound protein was eluted in resuspension buffer containing 250 mM imidazole. The proteins were further purified by SEC using the BioRad NGC Quest10 Chromatography system equipped with the Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 column in SEC buffer (25 mM HEPES (pH 7.4), 500 mM NaCl). The elution fractions were analyzed using SDS–PAGE followed by InstantBlue staining. Finally, the protein was concentrated by centrifugal ultrafiltration using an Amicon Ultra-15 centrifugal filter unit with a 10 kDa cut-off. Glycerol was added to a total concentration of 10% and aliquots were snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C.

Protein concentrations were determined by measuring the absorbance of the protein solution at 280 nm on a NanoDrop spectrophotometer and corrected by the protein-specific extinction coefficient.

#### In vitro Phosphorylation Assays

1 μg of recombinant GST-TBK1 protein was mixed with 2 μg of recombinant substrate in a 100 μL reaction buffer containing 20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.4, 5 mM ATP, 10 nM MgCl2, and 1 mM DTT and incubated for 1 hour at 30°C. Phoshorylation reactions were reversed by the addition of 10X Protein MetalloPhosphatase buffer, 1 mM MnCl2, and 200 units of λ-Protein Phosphatase. The reactions were stopped by adding 5x Laemmli buffer and boiling at 100°C for 5 min. Phosphorylation products were separated by SDS-PAGE and analyzed by immunoblotting.

#### Mass Spectrometry

Following the in vitro phosphorylation reaction, the products were separated by SDS-PAGE and the gel was stained with InstantBlue. The gel bands were excised and cut into approximately 1 mm3 pieces. The samples were reduced with 1 mM DTT for 30 minutes at 60°C and then alkylated with 5mM iodoacetamide for 15 minutes in the dark at room temperature. Gel pieces were washed and dehydrated with acetonitrile for 10 min, followed by removal of acetonitrile. The pieces were completely dried in a speed-vac and then rehydrated with 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate solution containing 12.5 ng/μL modified sequencing-grade trypsin (for STING and IRSp53) or chymotrypsin (for GMIP) at 4°C. Samples were then placed in a 37°C room overnight. Next, peptides were extracted, dissolved in 5 μL of HPLC solvent A, and pressure loaded off-line onto a nano-scale reverse-phase HPLC capillary column. Eluted peptides were analyzed in an LTQ-Orbitrap mass spectrometer (ThermoFinnigan). The modification of 79.9663 mass units to serine, threonine, and tyrosine was included in the database searches to determine phosphopeptides. The spectra for each phosphopeptide that was determined by the SEQUEST program was also manually inspected to ensure confidence. Phosphorylation sites with a ModScore of 19 or higher were considered confidently assigned with a p-value of >0.01.

#### Native-PAGE

For Native-PAGE analysis of nanomachine oligomerization, 1 × 106 iBMDMs were stimulated with 1 μM B/B for indicated times, and subsequently lysed in 200 μL of lysis buffer containing 25 mM TRIS pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, and 0.05% Triton-X 100. The lysates were centrifuged at 20,000 x g for 15 minutes at 4°C, and the cleared supernatants were transferred to new tubes. The 4X NativePAGE 5% G-250 sample buffer was added to the samples, which were run on a NativePAGE 4–16% Bis-Tris Gel using the NativePAGE Novex Bis-Tris Kit running buffers. The gel was then analyzed by western blot, with the transfer performed overnight at 4°C at 40V to ensure the transfer of large complexes.

#### Fluorescence Microscopy

For confocal imaging of nanomachine oligomerization, glass coverslips were placed in a 24-well plate prior to seeding 3 × 105 cells per well. Cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde at room temperature for 20 min, permeabilized with 0.2% Triton X-100 at room temperature for 10 min, and blocked with 1% bovine serine albumin at room temperature for 10 min. Primary antibody staining was performed with 50 μL of 1:100 mouse anti-FLAG antibody overnight at 4°C. Secondary antibody staining was performed with 50 μL of 1:400 anti-mouse A647 antibody for 1 hour at room temperature. 50 μL of 1:1000 DAPI was stained for 5 min. Coverslips were mounted using Prolong mounting medium and imaged with the Zeiss 880 laser scanning confocal microscope. Images were processed with the Zen 3.5 software. Representative images were chosen from at least three randomly chosen fields from one representative experiment of three independent experiments.

#### Bacterial Infection

Citrobacter rodentium was inoculated into 20 mL of high-glucose DMEM and allowed to grow statically at 37°C and 5% CO2 overnight. The next day, bacteria were diluted 1:10 into 20 mL of DMEM and allowed to expand for 3 hours. The optical density at 600 nm was determined and bacteria were diluted to an MOI of 1 in complete DMEM without antibiotics. Pre-seeded iBMDMs were washed with PBS and then infected with 1 mL of the diluted C. rodentium, centrifuged at 400 x g for 5 min, and incubated for 1 hour. Cells were then washed with PBS, and the media was replaced with complete DMEM supplemented with 10 μg/mL gentamicin. Cells were allowed to incubate for 23 additional hours and then supernatants were collected for analysis.

#### VLP Psuedotransduction

To generate viral-like particles (VLPs) 52, 2.5 × 106 293T cells were seeded and then transfected with pCL-Eco and VSV-G vectors. The media was replaced after 6 hours, and the supernatants were collected 24 hours later. They were spun down at 400 x g for 5 min, and the supernatants were filtered through a 0.45 μm PVDF filter via syringe into Beckman tubes. To prep the VLPs of contaminating DNA, they were spun at 53,200 x g for 90 min at 4°C. The supernatant was decanted, and the viral pellet was slowly resuspended in 1 mL NTE buffer (0.1 M sodium chloride, 1 mM EDTA, and 0.01 M Tris, pH 7.4) overnight at 4°C. The resuspended virus was then layered over a 15% sucrose cushion and pelleted at 47,000 rpm for 1 hr at 4°C using a Beckman rotor Type 70.1Ti. The pelleted virus was slowly resuspended by incubating the pellets in 1 mL NTE buffer overnight at 4°C. Polybrene (5 μg/ml) was added to the VLPs, and the supernatants were then used to pseudotransduce iBMDMs via spin-fection at 1250 x g for 60 min at 30°C.

#### Bulk RNA-sequencing

All RNA samples were collected based on QIAsymphony RNA protocol. Cells were lysed in 400 μL Buffer RLT Plus with 1% β-mercaptoethanol and stored at −80°C. Then, RNA for each sample was extracted using QIAsymphony RNA Isolation Kits on the QIAsymphony SP instrument. On the QIAsymphony, the RNA CT 400 protocol was selected and used for RNA isolation. The instrument was set up according to the manufacturer’s protocol and the elution volume for RNA samples was set to 100 μL.

For each sample, 500ng of total RNA was used for RNA-seq libraries construction. RNA-seq libraries were prepared by using KAPA RNA HyperPrep Kits. The library preparation method was tested manually and subsequently fully automated on the Biomek i7 Workstation. All prepared libraries were sequenced on NovaSeq6000 (Illumina) to generate 75 base paired ends and each depth of coverage: 50 million reads per sample.

The raw reads were aligned to the mouse genome (GRCm39) downloaded from Gencode using the STAR aligner (version-2.7.5c) 74. FeatureCounts function from the subread package (version 1.6.0) 79 was used to count the number of reads mapped to genomic features. The count matrix was imported into R. Trimmed Mean of M-values (TMM) (package edgeR) 75 was applied to the counts after filtering of low expressed genes. The outliers were removed using principal component analysis and hierarchical clustering of samples. Differential gene expression analysis was performed using the limma package in R76. An adjusted p-value <= 0.05 (Benjamini-Hochberg method) and a log2FC threshold of +/− 1 were used as cut-offs for determining differentially expressed genes (DEGs).

To observe the change in kinetics downstream upon modification of the pLxIS domain, for each WT nanomachine, top DEGs at each time point (2 hr, 4 hr, 6 hr, 8 hr, 16 hr) vs. untreated (0 hr) were combined. Heatplots were generated for all timepoints for both wildtype and respective mutated nanomachines for parallel comparison. To compare the transcriptional differences between the synthetic nanomachines, top DEGs at 8 hr vs. baseline for each nanomachine were combined and plotted for all five nanomachines. Over representation analysis was performed on the DEG lists, created by comparing each time points of all nanomachines to the respective negative control empty vector, using the clusterProfiler package in R77. For each nanomachine, significantly represented pathways (adj P-value <=0.05) for all time points were combined. These lists were used to identify common and unique pathways between nanomachines. To create the emapplot, the genes were also combined.

To compare the activation status of various transcription factors at each time point between WT/unmutated nanomachines, the DGE analysis was performed between each pair of nanomachines at each time point (example: Sting_2hrs vs. TRIF_2hrs, Sting_4hrs vs. TRIF_4hrs and so on). Upstream regulator analysis was done on the DEGS for each pair of nanomachine at each time point using Ingenuity pathway analysis(IPA) 80. The activation scores were compared at each timepoint relative to each nanomachine.

#### Seahorse Metabolic Analysis

Extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) was measured from LPS- and B/B-stimulated iBMDMs with a Seahorse XFe96 Extracellular Flux Analyzer instrument81. For real-time measurement of ECAR, 5 × 104 iBMDMs per well were seeded in a seahorse 96 well plate in complete DMEM medium. #### Metabolomics

At the end of the time course, cells were washed once with ice-cold PBS and another time with ice-cold 150 mM sodium chloride dissolved in LC/MS grade water. Samples were then immediately frozen in a bath of liquid nitrogen. To extract metabolites, 1 mL of −20°C 80% methanol solvent was added to each well and collected in a Safe-lock Eppendorf tube. Samples were vortexed for 15 minutes at 4°C and centrifuged at 21,000 x g for 15 min at 4°C. The supernatant containing polar metabolites was concentrated and dried using a 4°C CentriVap SpeedVac (Labconco). The dried extracts were then reconstituted in 1:1 acetonitrile:water for analysis on the MS. Samples were run on a Vanquish UHPLC system (Thermo Fisher) coupled to a Q-Exactive HF-X mass spectrometer utilizing a HESI probe (Thermo Fisher) in negative ion mode. For the LC, hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC) column was used, specifically a 150 X 2.1 mm iHILIC1-(P) Classic polymeric column equipped with a 2.1 × 20 mm iHILIC1-(P) Classic Guard column (both 5 μm, 200 Å, HILICON AB). Buffer A (20 mM ammonium carbonate in water, with 0.1% ammonium hydroxide) and buffer B (100% acetonitrile) were used. A linear gradient was performed at a flow rate of 0.15 ml/min as follows: 0–23 min linear gradient from 95% B to 5% B; 23–25 min hold at 5% B, to waste from 25–25.5 min gradient to 95% B at 0.20 mL/min, 25.5–32.5 min hold at 95% B, and finally 32.5–33 min 95% B at 0.15 mL/min. The column was held at 25 °C, the column preheater at 30°C and the autosampler at 4°C. MS acquisition was performed on full scan mode over a range of 70–1000 m/z and a resolution of 60,000, an AGC target of 1e5 and a maximum injection time of 20 ms with a 5 eV in-source CID. The spray voltage was set to 3 kV, the heated capillary was set at 275°C and the probe was set at 350°C. The sheath gas flow rate was 40, the auxiliary gas was set at 15, and the sweep gas flow rate was set to 1. Peak integration was performed using Tracefinder version 4.1. Metabolites were identified using exact mass with a 5 ppm tolerance and retention time with reference to an in-house library of chemical standards. Peaks were manually curated to exclude low-quality peaks (e.g., noise, multiple peaks) and metabolites with no identifiable peaks, resulting in a list of 118 confirmed metabolites. Values were normalized to cell count.

#### Viral Infection and Plaque Assays

For infection of MTSM KO cells with Sendai virus, SeV was diluted to an MOI of 0.00001 in DMEM with 1% FBS and 500 μL of the diluted virus was added to cells. The plate was agitated every 15 min and then the media was replaced after 1 hour. For infection of A549s with VSV or IAV PR8, virus was diluted in complete DMEM (10% FBS) to an MOI of 1 for VSV or an MOI of 0.1 for IAV. The cells were inoculated with 300 μL of virus in a 6 well plate, the plate was agitated every 15 min, and then the media was replaced after 1 hour.

To perform a plaque assay of VSV, 4 × 105 Vero cells were seeded the day before in 6 well plates. Serial dilutions of viral supernatants were prepared in complete DMEM and 300 μL was added to infect the Vero cells. The plates were agitated every 15 min and then after 1 hour the virus inoculum was replaced with 2 mL of 2.5% carboxymethylcellulose (diluted in complete DMEM from 5% stock). Plates were incubated for 2 days and then plaques were resolved with 1 mL of 0.25% Coomassie Blue in 10% acetic acid and 45% methanol at room temp for 10 min. To perform a plaque assay of IAV, 1.2 × 106 MDCK cells were seeded the day before in 6 well plates. Serial dilutions of viral supernatants were prepared in influenza infection media (IMDM with L-glutamine/HEPES, 1% Pen/Strep, 0.2% BSA, and 2 μg/mL TPCK-treated trypsin) and 300 μL was added to infect the MDCK cells. The plates were agitated every 15 min and then after 1 hour the virus inoculum was replaced with 2 mL of 0.3% agarose in influenza infection media. Plates were incubated for 2 days and then cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 1 hour at 4°C and plaques were resolved with 1 mL of 1% crystal violet in 20% ethanol at room temp for 10 min.

### QUANTIFICATION AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS

Statistical significance for experiments with multiple groups and multiple independent variables were tested with two-way ANOVA with uncorrected Fisher’s LSD test. One-way ANOVA with Fisher’s LSD test was used for analysis of multiple groups with a single independent variable. An unpaired two-tailed t test was used for comparison of two groups. Adjusted p-values were calculated with Prism 9.4 from GraphPad and the designation of * corresponds to p ≤ 0.05, ** corresponds to p ≤ 0.01, *** corresponds to p ≤ 0.001, and **** corresponds to a p ≤ 0.0001 in the figures. Data presented is representative of at least 3 independent experiments for western blots and bar graphs. Data with error bars are represented as mean ± SEM.
